lessons.title: Choosing the Right Tomato Varieties for Paste and Sauce
lessons.body:
For tomato paste and sauce, you need tomatoes that are meaty, low in water, and high in natural sugars and acids. In Africa, the best varieties are often local landraces like 'Tengeru' in Tanzania, 'Marmande' in South Africa, or improved types such as 'Roma VF', 'UC82B', and 'Petomech'. These are determinate (bush) types that ripen all at once, making harvest and processing easier. Avoid watery salad tomatoes like 'Money Maker' â they give thin paste and need more cooking, which wastes fuel.

When selecting seeds or seedlings, look for varieties with resistance to local diseases like bacterial wilt and early blight. In West Africa, 'Ibadan Local' is popular for its deep red colour and thick walls. In East Africa, 'Tanya' is a good choice for paste because it has few seeds and high solids. If you are buying from a market, ask the seller which variety they have. If they don't know, look for tomatoes that are oval or pear-shaped, not round and juicy.

For sauce, you can use slightly softer tomatoes, but they should still be firm and ripe. A good rule: 1 kg of Roma tomatoes yields about 700 g of usable pulp after peeling and seeding. If you use watery tomatoes, you might only get 500 g. That difference matters for your profit. Also, consider colour: deep red tomatoes have more lycopene, which gives paste its rich colour. Pale or greenish tomatoes will make dull paste.

If you grow your own, plant determinate varieties in blocks, not rows, so they support each other. Space them 60 cm apart. Apply compost or NPK 17-17-17 at planting. Harvest when fruits are fully red but still firm. For paste, pick all at once when 90% are ripe. For sauce, you can harvest every 2-3 days. Never mix varieties in one batch â they cook at different rates and give inconsistent texture.

Finally, test a small batch before committing. Boil 2 kg of tomatoes for 30 minutes, then strain. If you get at least 1.2 kg of thick pulp, the variety is good for paste. If it's watery, use it for juice or sauce instead. Remember: the right variety is the foundation of good paste and sauce.

lessons.title: How to Test Tomato Quality: Firmness, Colour, and Sweetness
lessons.body:
Before you buy or process tomatoes, test them for firmness, colour, and sweetness. These three factors determine your final product's taste, texture, and shelf life. Start with firmness: gently squeeze a tomato in your palm. It should feel heavy for its size and give slightly, like a ripe avocado. If it's rock hard, it's unripe and will be acidic. If it's mushy, it's overripe and will spoil quickly. For paste, you want firm-ripe tomatoes. For sauce, you can use slightly softer ones, but never use tomatoes with soft spots or mould.

Colour is next. A good tomato is uniformly red from stem to bottom. Green shoulders mean it was picked too early; it will lack sweetness and have a bitter taste. Yellow or orange patches mean it's not fully ripe. For paste, deep red is best because it indicates high lycopene. Hold the tomato against a light â if you see dark spots inside, discard it. Also check the skin: it should be smooth and shiny, not wrinkled or cracked. Cracks let in bacteria.

Sweetness is measured with a refractometer, but you can also taste. Cut a wedge and chew it. A good paste tomato has a balance of sweet and tart, with a sugar content of at least 5% (5 Brix). If it tastes watery or bland, it won't make good paste. You can also use a simple float test: put tomatoes in a bucket of water. Those that sink are denser and better for paste; those that float are watery and better for juice. For sauce, you want a Brix of 4-5%.

In Africa, many markets sell tomatoes in bulk. Take a random sample of 10 tomatoes. Check each for firmness, colour, and taste. If more than 2 are bad, reject the lot or negotiate a lower price. Also, smell the tomatoes â they should smell sweet and earthy, not sour or fermented. If they smell like alcohol, they are rotting.

Finally, test acidity. High-acid tomatoes (pH below 4.6) are safer for canning. You can use pH strips. If pH is above 4.6, add lemon juice or citric acid when making sauce. For paste, you want pH 4.0-4.4. Remember: quality in, quality out. Spend time testing before you buy.

lessons.title: Washing and Sorting Tomatoes to Remove Dirt and Spoiled Fruits
lessons.body:
Washing and sorting are critical steps to prevent dirt, stones, and spoiled fruits from ruining your paste or sauce. Start by filling a large basin or drum with clean water. For 20 kg of tomatoes, use about 40 litres of water. Add 1 tablespoon of food-grade bleach (sodium hypochlorite) per 10 litres to kill bacteria, or use 2 tablespoons of salt per 10 litres. Never use soap or detergent â it leaves residue.

Sort tomatoes before washing. Remove any with mould, deep cracks, bird pecks, or soft spots. Also remove green tomatoes, leaves, and stems. A good rule: discard at least 5% of the harvest. If you have 100 kg, expect to throw away 5 kg. Do this on a clean tarpaulin or table, not on the ground. Wear gloves to protect your hands from acids and dirt.

Wash in three stages. First, dump tomatoes into the first basin and swirl gently for 2 minutes. This removes loose dirt. Then transfer to a second basin with clean water and 1 tablespoon of bleach per 10 litres. Soak for 5 minutes. Finally, rinse in a third basin with clean water. Never reuse dirty water â it spreads bacteria. Change water every 20 kg of tomatoes.

After washing, inspect each tomato again. Cut out any remaining bad spots with a clean knife. If a tomato is more than 20% spoiled, discard it. For paste, you need perfect fruits. For sauce, you can use slightly blemished ones, but still remove all mould. Mould produces mycotoxins that survive cooking.

Dry the tomatoes on a clean rack or cloth for 10 minutes before peeling. This prevents water from diluting your paste. If you are processing immediately, you can skip drying, but excess water means longer cooking time and more fuel. Always wash your hands, knives, and basins with soap and hot water before starting. Sanitation is key to a safe product. In Africa, where water can be scarce, use the three-basin method to save water while still getting clean tomatoes.

lessons.title: Blanching and Peeling Tomatoes for Smooth Paste
lessons.body:
Blanching and peeling tomatoes is essential for smooth paste. The skin is tough and bitter; if left on, it makes paste gritty and dark. Blanching also loosens the skin and kills surface bacteria. Here's how to do it with basic tools: a large pot, a slotted spoon, a bowl of ice water (or cold water), and a knife.

First, bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. For 5 kg of tomatoes, use about 10 litres of water. While waiting, cut a shallow 'X' on the bottom of each tomato. This helps the skin split. When the water boils, drop 5-6 tomatoes into the pot at a time. Do not overcrowd. Boil for 30-60 seconds â just until you see the skin start to curl and pull away from the flesh. Over-blanching cooks the tomato and makes it mushy.

Immediately transfer the tomatoes to a bowl of ice water or very cold water. This stops the cooking and makes them cool enough to handle. Let them sit for 2 minutes. Then, using your hands or a small knife, peel the skin off. It should slip off easily. If it doesn't, blanch for another 15 seconds. Put the peeled tomatoes in a clean bowl. Discard the skins or save them for other products (see Lesson 6).

For large-scale processing, you can use a steam blancher or a perforated basket. But for small businesses, the pot method works fine. Work in batches of 5 kg to keep the water hot. Change the water every 10 kg, or when it becomes cloudy. Add a little salt (1 tablespoon per litre) to the blanching water to help firm the flesh.

After peeling, remove the hard core with a knife. For paste, you want only the soft flesh. You can also squeeze out some seeds and juice. For every 1 kg of peeled tomatoes, you should have about 800 g of usable flesh. If you have less, you over-blanched. Practice makes perfect. Remember: blanching time depends on tomato size. Small cherry tomatoes need only 20 seconds; large Roma tomatoes need 60 seconds. Always test one tomato first.

lessons.title: De-seeding and Chopping for Chunky Sauces
lessons.body:
For chunky sauces, you want pieces of tomato, not a smooth paste. De-seeding and chopping are done after peeling. Start with peeled tomatoes. Cut each tomato in half horizontally (across the middle). Use your thumb or a small spoon to scoop out the seeds and watery gel into a bowl. Save this â you can use it for juice or stock. For a chunky sauce, you want to remove most seeds because they add bitterness and make the sauce gritty.

Once de-seeded, chop the tomato flesh into cubes. For a rustic sauce, chop into 1-2 cm pieces. For a finer sauce, chop into 0.5 cm pieces. Use a sharp knife on a clean cutting board. A dull knife crushes the tomato and makes it mushy. Work quickly to avoid losing juice. If you are processing many tomatoes, use a manual food chopper or a stainless steel grater. But a knife gives better control.

For 5 kg of peeled tomatoes, you should get about 3.5 kg of chopped flesh after de-seeding. The seeds and gel make up about 30% of the weight. If you want a thicker sauce, let the chopped tomatoes sit in a colander for 10 minutes to drain excess water. Save that water for soups.

In Africa, many traditional sauces use onions, peppers, and oil. Add these after chopping. For a chunky tomato sauce, sautÃ© onions and peppers first, then add the chopped tomatoes. Cook for 20-30 minutes until the sauce thickens. Do not overcook â you want visible pieces. If you want a smoother sauce, blend half of the chopped tomatoes and mix back in.

Always taste the chopped tomatoes. If they are too acidic, add a pinch of sugar. If too sweet, add a squeeze of lemon. For canning, add 1 tablespoon of lemon juice per 500 ml jar to ensure safety. Remember: de-seeding and chopping are about texture. For paste, you skip this step and blend everything. For sauce, you want chunks. Adjust your chop size to your market â some customers prefer large pieces, others small.

lessons.title: Reducing Waste: Using Tomato Skins and Seeds for Other Products
lessons.body:
Tomato skins and seeds are not waste â they are valuable resources. After peeling and de-seeding, you can turn them into three products: tomato powder, tomato oil, and animal feed. This reduces waste and increases your profit. For every 10 kg of tomatoes, you get about 1 kg of skins and 0.5 kg of seeds. Don't throw them away.

First, tomato powder. Spread the skins on a clean tray and dry them in the sun for 2-3 days, or in a solar dryer for 6-8 hours. They should be brittle. Grind them in a blender or with a mortar and pestle. Sift to remove large pieces. The powder is rich in lycopene and fibre. Use it to thicken soups, stews, or even as a natural food colouring. Store in an airtight jar for up to 6 months. You can sell 100 g for about $2.

Second, tomato seed oil. Dry the seeds completely, then grind them. Mix with a little water and boil, then skim off the oil that floats. Or use a manual oil press. Tomato seed oil is rich in antioxidants and good for skin. You can also roast the dried seeds and eat them as a snack, or grind them into a protein-rich flour for animal feed. For chickens, mix 10% tomato seed meal into their feed. It improves egg yolk colour.

Third, animal feed. Mix dried skins and seeds with other food scraps (cassava peels, maize bran) and feed to pigs, goats, or chickens. This saves money on commercial feed. Ensure the mixture is dry to prevent mould. You can also compost the skins and seeds to make organic fertiliser for your next tomato crop. Compost them with dry leaves and manure. Turn every week. In 2 months, you have rich compost.

Finally, use the seed gel (the watery part around seeds) as a natural fertiliser spray. Dilute 1 part gel with 5 parts water and spray on plants. It contains nutrients and beneficial microbes. So, instead of throwing away 15% of your tomato weight, you create extra products. This is how you turn a small tomato business into a profitable one. Always keep your processing area clean and dry to avoid pests.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Selecting and Preparing Raw Materials for Tomato Paste & Sauce

In tomato processing, raw material selection and preparation determine up to 60â70% of final product quality and cost. For African agribusinesses â whether you are a smallholder aggregator supplying a processor, or running a 500 kg/hour paste line â the decisions you make between harvest and the blanching tank directly control your yield per tonne, your colour score, your brix recovery, and your margin. This practical reference consolidates the technical benchmarks you need to buy, test, and prepare tomatoes with confidence.

1. Choosing the Right Tomato Varieties

For paste, you need high brix, high viscosity, high colour, and determinate bearing. Roma, UC82B, Petomech, and locally adapted lines such as Padma and Nadira (bred for West African conditions) are standard. For sauce, slightly lower brix is acceptable but flavour and fleshiness matter more.

Source: Codex Alimentarius CODEX STAN 57-1981; FAO Agricultural Services Bulletin 148 (2004).

2. Testing Tomato Quality: Firmness, Colour, Sweetness

Field testing protects your processing line. A simple three-test protocol:

  • Firmness: Squeeze test â ripe tomatoes should yield slightly but not collapse. For accuracy, use a handheld penetrometer (target 1.5â2.5 kg/cmÂ²).
  • Colour: Cut cross-section; internal colour must match external. Reject green-shouldered or white-cored fruit.
  • Sweetness: Refractometer reading on a drop of juice. Below 4.0Â°Brix means poor paste yield.

3. Washing and Sorting

Dirt, stones, and spoiled fruit destroy equipment and flavour. Use a three-stage wash: dry brush â spray wash â final rinse with 50â100 ppm chlorinated water. Sort on a roller or vibrating table with 4â6 workers removing green, rotten, insect-damaged, and foreign material.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Chlorine and Lye Handling

When using chlorinated wash water or sodium hydroxide (lye) for peeling, always wear chemical splash goggles, nitrile gloves, and a face shield. Lye at 10â20% concentration causes severe burns and can blind. Ensure adequate ventilation, never add water to lye (add lye to water), and keep an eyewash station within 10 metres of the peeling line. Store chemicals locked away from food contact surfaces.

4. Blanching and Peeling

Blanching at 85â95Â°C for 2â4 minutes loosens skins, inactivates enzymes (polyphenol oxidase, pectin methylesterase), and improves colour retention. Over-blanching causes mush and nutrient loss; under-blanching causes poor peel and enzymatic browning.

Source: FAO Agricultural Services Bulletin 148 (2004), Table 4.3; adapted for African SME conditions.

5. De-seeding and Chopping for Chunky Sauces

For chunky sauce, de-seed by cutting tomatoes in half and gently squeezing or using a pulper with a 8â10 mm screen. Chop to 8â12 mm cubes for a visible, premium texture. For paste, seeds and skins are removed entirely before concentration.

6. Reducing Waste: Using Skins and Seeds

Tomato processing generates 3â5% skin and 2â3% seed waste. In Africa, these are revenue opportunities:

  • Skins: Rich in lycopene and pectin â extract pectin for jam/gummy production, or dry and mill for animal feed supplement.
  • Seeds: Contain 20â25% oil (high in linoleic acid) â cold-press for cosmetic or cooking oil. Seed meal is a protein-rich animal feed (30â35% protein).
  • Trim & pulp: Use for juice, ketchup base, or compost.

A 1 t/day paste line can generate 40â60 kg of skins and 25â35 kg of seeds daily â enough to justify a small by-product sideline.

  3. â Check colour: no green shoulders, uniform red inside and out.
  4. â Squeeze test: firm but yielding; reject soft or water-soaked fruit.
  5. â Wash in 3 stages; final rinse at 50â100 ppm chlorine.
  6. â Sort out rotten, insect-damaged, and green fruit before blanching.
  7. â Blanch at 85â95Â°C for 2â4 minutes â use a timer, not guesswork.
  8. â Segregate skins and seeds for by-product income, not the bin.

quiz.q: Which type of tomato is best for making paste?
options: B) Meaty, low-water varieties like Roma
quiz.explanation: Meaty, low-water varieties like Roma yield thicker paste with less cooking.

quiz.q: What is a good yield of usable pulp from 1 kg of Roma tomatoes after peeling and seeding?
quiz.explanation: Roma tomatoes typically yield about 700 g of usable pulp per kg.

quiz.q: Which variety is mentioned as good for paste in East Africa?
quiz.explanation: Tanya is noted for few seeds and high solids, good for paste in East Africa.

quiz.q: What does a float test tell you about tomatoes?
options: B) Their density and suitability for paste
quiz.explanation: Tomatoes that sink are denser and better for paste; those that float are watery.

quiz.q: What is the minimum Brix (sugar content) for a good paste tomato?
quiz.explanation: A good paste tomato should have at least 5% sugar (5 Brix).

quiz.q: How many tomatoes out of a sample of 10 should be bad before you reject the lot?
quiz.explanation: If more than 2 out of 10 are bad, reject the lot or negotiate a lower price.

quiz.q: What is the ideal pH range for tomato paste?
quiz.explanation: Tomato paste should have a pH of 4.0-4.4 for safety and taste.

quiz.q: How much food-grade bleach should you add per 10 litres of water for washing tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: 1 tablespoon of food-grade bleach per 10 litres kills bacteria without harming tomatoes.

quiz.q: What percentage of tomatoes should you expect to discard during sorting?
quiz.explanation: Expect to discard at least 5% of the harvest due to spoilage or defects.

quiz.q: Why should you not use soap or detergent to wash tomatoes?
options: D) It makes them too slippery
quiz.explanation: Soap and detergent leave residue that can be harmful if consumed.

quiz.q: How many stages should washing tomatoes involve?
quiz.explanation: A three-stage wash (rinse, bleach soak, final rinse) ensures cleanliness.

quiz.q: What should you do with tomatoes that are more than 20% spoiled?
options: B) Cut out bad parts and use
quiz.explanation: Tomatoes more than 20% spoiled should be discarded to avoid mycotoxins.

quiz.q: Why is it important to dry tomatoes after washing?
options: A) To prevent water from diluting the paste
B) To make them easier to peel
quiz.explanation: Excess water dilutes the paste and increases cooking time and fuel use.

quiz.q: How long should you blanch tomatoes in boiling water?
quiz.explanation: Blanching for 30-60 seconds loosens the skin without cooking the flesh.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of cutting an 'X' on the bottom of tomatoes before blanching?
options: A) To make them look pretty
B) To help the skin split
quiz.explanation: The 'X' helps the skin split and peel easily after blanching.

quiz.q: After blanching, what should you do immediately?
options: A) Put tomatoes in ice water
quiz.explanation: Ice water stops the cooking process and makes them cool enough to handle.

quiz.q: How much salt can you add to blanching water to help firm the flesh?
quiz.explanation: 1 tablespoon of salt per litre of blanching water helps firm the tomato flesh.

quiz.q: What is the approximate yield of peeled tomatoes from 1 kg of whole tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: About 800 g of peeled tomatoes are obtained from 1 kg of whole tomatoes.

quiz.q: Why should you remove seeds when making chunky sauce?
options: A) Seeds add bitterness and grittiness
C) Seeds make sauce too sweet
D) Seeds are hard to digest
quiz.explanation: Seeds can add bitterness and make the sauce gritty, so they are removed.

quiz.q: What size should you chop tomatoes for a rustic chunky sauce?
quiz.explanation: For a rustic sauce, chop into 1-2 cm pieces for visible chunks.

quiz.q: How much of a peeled tomato is made up of seeds and gel?
quiz.explanation: Seeds and gel make up about 30% of the weight of peeled tomatoes.

quiz.q: What can you add to chunky sauce if it is too acidic?
quiz.explanation: A pinch of sugar balances the acidity in tomato sauce.

quiz.q: How much lemon juice should you add per 500 ml jar of sauce for canning?
quiz.explanation: 1 tablespoon of lemon juice per 500 ml jar ensures safe acidity for canning.

quiz.q: What is a good use for tomato skins after peeling?
quiz.explanation: Dried and ground tomato skins make a nutritious tomato powder.

quiz.q: How long should you dry tomato skins in the sun to make powder?
quiz.explanation: Sun-drying tomato skins for 2-3 days makes them brittle enough to grind.

quiz.q: What is tomato seed oil good for?
quiz.explanation: Tomato seed oil is rich in antioxidants and good for skin care.

quiz.q: How much tomato seed meal can you mix into chicken feed?
quiz.explanation: Up to 10% tomato seed meal can be mixed into chicken feed.

quiz.q: What can you do with the seed gel from tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Diluted seed gel can be used as a natural fertiliser spray for plants.

quiz.q: How often should you turn compost made from tomato waste?
quiz.explanation: Turning compost every week speeds up decomposition and reduces odour.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of reducing waste from tomato processing?
quiz.explanation: Using skins and seeds for other products increases overall profit from the same tomatoes.
